Threehalves is a 7-foot-tall, four-legged "centaur" robot built by Satyress Robotics (a project led by an engineer named Beau based out of Auburn, California). It went viral on social media due to its imposing, demonic aesthetic—featuring a goat-like horned head, glowing eyes, and modular arms that can mount power tools like chainsaws. #foryou #fyp #threehalves #satyressrobotics #robot #ai #centaurrobot #edit #trending #keşfet #freegaza #freepalestine #creppy #scary

Everyone's calling this thing demonic. There's no AI in it. It's called Threehalves, built by a California startup called Satyress. Two meters tall, and it's meant to walk into wildfires and collapsed buildings so a person doesn't have to. Nobody's inside it. A guy drives it with a joystick from a safe distance. It has no hands at all — the wrists take a chainsaw or a drill instead. The brakes run on air, and if it loses pressure they clamp on by themselves, which is why the company published a diagram telling you where to puncture it if you need it to stop. It also can't turn around in a hallway. No price, no release date, and most of the pictures going around are renders. #threehalves #satyress #rescuerobot #centaurrobot #sucklessai

XPENG’s humanoid robot, known as IRON, represents the company’s expansion beyond electric vehicles into robotics and embodied AI. XPENG, a Chinese EV manufacturer founded in 2014, has leveraged its expertise in electric drivetrains, AI software, and autonomous systems to develop robotic platforms capable of dynamic movement and real-time environmental interaction. Humanoid robots like IRON rely on advanced motion planning algorithms, electric actuators, and sensor fusion systems - typically combining cameras, LiDAR, inertial measurement units (IMUs), and force sensors. These systems allow the robot to maintain balance, adjust posture, and perform coordinated movements that appear fluid and human-like. Modern humanoid locomotion depends heavily on real-time feedback control. Small positional corrections are made hundreds of times per second to stabilize joints and prevent falls. This is similar to the control architecture used in self-balancing robots and autonomous vehicles. XPENG’s broader robotics initiative aligns with a global push toward general-purpose humanoid platforms - machines designed to operate in human environments rather than factory-only settings. While still in early development stages, such robots are being researched for applications ranging from logistics and manufacturing to service roles and human-robot interaction studies.
